d3de6a4a40bd3f8b.subject: CoreWeave Is a Cloud Company. Its Economics Are a Spread Trade
d3de6a4a40bd3f8b.body:
View this post on the web at https://gadallon.substack.com/p/coreweave-is-a-cloud-company-its

If there is one firm I’m constantly being asked about, it’s CoreWeave.
Operationally, CoreWeave is a cloud company, and a very good one
Economically, it is a financed infrastructure book.
This newsletter usually studies the former. This time I have to take the latter.
Q2, reported a few days ago on August 11 [ https://substack.com/redirect/369a054c-a761-4f72-9244-492098e17888?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], put the entire model in a single margin waterfall: Revenue of $2.575 billion, up 112%. Adjusted EBITDA margin of 59%. After depreciation, the adjusted operating margin is 5%. After stock compensation and other adjustments, the GAAP operating margin is negative 2%. After $640 million of interest expense, the GAAP net margin is negative 24%. The stock jumped 13% after hours anyway.
The gap between those figures does not account for noise. This is the business.
I know everyone is focusing on the backlog, but the $104 billion backlog is the least informative headline number CoreWeave publishes, but it is the one the market trades on.
The after-hours move I mentioned above priced the contracts. But as I am going to discuss, the value ( if any) lies in the renewals.
CoreWeave is the purest public instrument of the AI buildout, and a generation of investors is learning infrastructure economics from this one ticker.  It is quite telling that people hold it up as proof that compute is the new oil.
But, the company’s structure supports a more rigorous analysis.
The Trade Behind the Company
The conventional narrative is that CoreWeave is a small hyperscaler that got to Nvidia’s newest silicon faster than Amazon and Microsoft.
And as always, there is truth in that. But as usual, it is not sufficient.
Before CoreWeave was a cloud company, it was Atlantic Crypto, an Ethereum mining shop founded in 2017. And before the founders were crypto miners, they were commodity traders. Michael Intrator ran a natural gas hedge fund. Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee came out of the same world of basis risk, storage spreads, and take-or-pay contracts.
The company they built still runs like a book of trades: Borrow. Buy silicon from a single supplier. Lease it to a handful of counterparties on multi-year take-or-pay contracts. Collect the difference.
Wall Street calls this a hyperscaler or neocloud. But a gas trader would recognize the play immediately: a financed basis trade with a data center wrapped around it.
That framing may sound like an insult, but believe me: It is not. Some of the best businesses in history are spread businesses; banking is a spread business.
The machine (or business equation of the firm) reduces to five lines:
Contracted revenue
	minus power, leases, and operating costs
	minus economic depreciation
equals the unlevered asset return,
	minus the cost of capital
equals value created for equity.
Everything else in the story, from deployment timing to utilization, useful life, renewal pricing, and customer concentration, is a claim about one of those lines.
The first three define the operating spread: what the assets earn before financing.
The last two define the financial spread: whether that return clears the cost of the money that built them.
Long-time readers know that I like to use my SCALE framework, but what follows is a SCALE analysis of the company, this time organized around the spread rather than the letters, because at CoreWeave, the letters keep collapsing into the same question.
The 59–5–Minus-24 Quarter (Scalable)
Revenue growth is not in question. The trajectory is close to unprecedented for a company this capital-heavy.
But scalable, in the SCALE sense, does not mean revenue grows. It means margins expand as revenue grows. I know I sound like a broken record, but I can’t tell you how many times a firm claims to have “economies of scale” when the data clearly indicates they don’t.
Let’s walk down the Q2 income statement: The adjusted EBITDA margin is 59% in the software segment. Depreciation and amortization take out roughly 54 points, leaving a 5% adjusted operating margin.
Stock compensation and other adjustments take out another 7, leaving GAAP operating income slightly negative.
Interest reduces the net margin to -24. Intrator called the quarter an inflection point, and the call [ https://substack.com/redirect/23d9c5fd-0e19-43a8-8373-09545ef45f77?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] backs him partway: $200 to $260 million of adjusted operating income guided for Q3, low-teens margins by Q4, new contracts signing at contribution margins five to ten points above recent cohorts.
The direction is clearly real, but the shape is unchanged: fifty-nine points before the machines are paid for, five points after.
Exhibit 1. Revenue vs. capex, 2024–2026E. 2024–25 are cash purchases of PP&E; 2026 guidance uses the company’s broader capex definition, which includes finance leases.
Exhibit 2. The Q2 2026 margin waterfall, in four steps.
At the guidance midpoints, 2026 capex is roughly 2.9 times 2026 revenue. That is not a unit-cost comparison; the assets will generate revenue for years to come. It measures how much capital the growth plan must absorb before the assets mature. It is also what a business looks like when the cost structure is the product. A software company adds a customer, and its servers barely notice. CoreWeave adds a customer and buys the customer’s infrastructure first, with borrowed money, then earns it back over the contract.
Each new dollar of revenue arrives with its own capex, depreciation schedule, and coupon payments. Volume goes up. Unit economics stay the same. That is throughput, not margin expansion.
The one number that behaves like a software company is the backlog: $15 billion, $66.8 billion, and $104.2 billion over six quarters, before the $25 billion added in early Q3, per the Q2 presentation [ https://substack.com/redirect/6583940c-f3c0-44bf-96f8-27d0910f9fed?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. The contracts scale. The conversion of contracts into margin has not yet occurred.
Exhibit 3. Contracts scale like software; revenue scales like infrastructure.
The Coupon Is Falling. The Interest Bill Is Rising (Constraint)
Tell me what constrains you, and I will tell you where your strategy should focus.
For CoreWeave, the constraint has moved three times in three years.
In 2023 it was chips, and the strategy was allocation: get closer to Nvidia than anyone else. That worked so well that Nvidia is now supplier, shareholder, and buyer of last resort through a $6.3 billion capacity backstop.
In 2024 and 2025 it was power. As of June 30, the company had 1.5 gigawatts active against 3.7 contracted, and it added roughly 500 megawatts more of contracted power in the six weeks after quarter-end, reaching 4.2.
The gap between contracted and active is the business plan, and every quarter of delay is a quarter in which capital sits on the balance sheet,t earning nothing.
By 2026, the binding constraint is the price of money, and the balance sheet has to be read the way a credit analyst would, in separate categories rather than as one scary number. As of June 30: $34.9 billion of debt. Another $16.3 billion in operating lease liabilities is already on the books, with a further $38.5 billion in payments on leases that have been signed but not yet commenced, per the 10-K [ https://substack.com/redirect/09e82a0c-37d7-4067-9d02-8d95da9a7a3a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Against that, $6.9 billion of cash and securities, $5 billion of equity, and one funding source people miss: $9.7 billion of deferred revenue, which is customers financing CoreWeave interest-free, in exchange for service obligations.
The first half’s cash flow statement describes the machine in

d00cd04bcbe8ca29.subject: Are movie end credits getting longer?
d00cd04bcbe8ca29.body:
View this post on the web at https://stephenfollows.com/p/are-movie-end-credits-getting-longer

I saw Spider-Man: Far From Necessary [ https://substack.com/redirect/a2b82ca9-cc37-48dc-9a7d-0c3597c30755?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] over the weekend and, like everyone else in the cinema, I sat through the entire end crawl to watch the ‘post-credits scene’ that has become so ubiquitous among superhero movies.
On the one hand, it’s great to see so many people get the recognition they deserve for working on such a big endeavour. On the other hand, I just wanted to get home.
But it reminded me of some research I conducted earlier in the year that I haven’t yet published.  I built a system to detect when the end credits begin in a movie and tracked the data for over 6,500 movies over the past 105 years of cinema.
How long are end credits these days?
Across all 6,515 films, the median end credits sequence runs 4 minutes 26 seconds. Half of all films sit between three and six minutes. 
If this feels unusually short to you, that’s because it’s changing.
Have end credits got longer?
In a word, yes. Spectacularly.
For most of cinema’s first seventy years, the end of a film was exactly that - it ended. A typical film of the 1930s, 40s or 50s ended with a cast reprise or a simple “The End” card (’Fin’ if you were fancy). The median credits length didn’t shift much over forty years, going from 25 seconds in the 1930s to just 34 seconds by the 1960s.
Long-time readers will spot my familiar refrain that “Something weird happened to cinema in the 1970s” and today we see yet another example. End credits changed dramatically, more than doubling in length within the decade, and then doubling again over the 1980s.
By the 1990s, end credits were 4 minutes long, and they've kept climbing ever since, reaching 5:43 for films released in the 2020s.
Current movie credits are almost thirteen times longer than those of the 1950s. 
Which films have the longest credits?
The films with the biggest budgets, unsurprisingly, have the longest credits.
Of everything I tested, production budget is the strongest predictor of credit length, at least for films made this century. This makes sense, as that's what they're spending all that money on - people, companies, vendors, etc
This is a fairly new correlation. We can use the Pearson correlation coefficient to give us a single number for how connected two sets of data are, with zero meaning no correlation and plus one meaning perfect positive correlation. 
There was no connection between credit length and production budgets in the middle of the last century (1960s = 0.08, 1970s = 0.07), but as credits got longer, the connection grew (1990s = 0.33, 2000s = 0.39) until the modern era, where it’s up to 0.5.
The same is true of the number of people involved. How many crew a film credits explains its credit length far better than how many actors it has (0.44 versus 0.18), and once you account for the crew, cast size tells you nothing at all.
Animations have the longest credits, with documentary credits having the shortest - just a third of their animated cousins. 
And when we drill deeper into the types of movies, we see an even clearer culprit - Marvel et al. Superhero films run a median of 7:09, compared with 5:08 for everything else. 
Why are credits getting longer?
The data can’t give us a definitive reason this is happening, but I think the four most likely causes are:
Freelancers need credits 
The credits moved
The VFX boom
Nobody is in charge
1. Freelancers need credits 
Under the old studio system, most film workers were salaried staff and simply weren’t named on screen. The Wizard of Oz (1939) ended with on-screen titles listing eleven names [ https://substack.com/redirect/615f173e-d7b2-445e-998e-1e507c216c58?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], and one of those was a dog.
The Paramount Decree of 1948 [ https://substack.com/redirect/d21f4d37-4c42-4c87-816b-8e597fe3b3d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] broke up the studios’ vertically integrated empires and the studios fired many of their permanent staff. Filmmaking shifted to a freelance, project-by-project business, meaning a screen credit became more important in securing the next job. 
2. The credits moved
As more people angled for an on-screen credit, the main roller had to move from before the film to after it. Until the late 1960s, credits mostly ran at the start of the film, where the audience had no choice but to sit through them, so they stayed short. 
Films like Around the World in 80 Days [ https://substack.com/redirect/88b17128-ebd2-41b5-ab1d-5d081a90160b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (1956), West Side Story [ https://substack.com/redirect/de263a27-9884-496c-83eb-aa1621fb6f49?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (1961) and 2001: A Space Odyssey [ https://substack.com/redirect/4193bc1e-0a25-4e6c-b442-fbe42f95b971?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (1968) pioneered pushing them to the end, and by the 1980s the modern pattern was standard. 
Once the names moved to the end, where nobody had to watch them, there was no longer any pressure to keep the list short. 
Industry guilds had a role in this. When The Empire Strikes Back [ https://substack.com/redirect/cc2f265d-c08b-48a1-bb3b-e82ac8f1e651?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (1980) opened without traditional front credits, the Directors Guild objected (their rules required the director’s name up front if anyone’s was there), and the guilds fined George Lucas a quarter of a million dollars [ https://substack.com/redirect/8ce3a7b6-7aae-4c40-b277-5659ba9d73ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. He paid up but called it extortion, and resigned from both the DGA and the WGA [ https://substack.com/redirect/8efb1e0c-aa03-447f-b24e-ac9373b6c73d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. 
The current rules that survive today mandate surprisingly little about end credits, other than the actors’ agreement, which requires that at least 50 cast members be listed in the end titles [ https://substack.com/redirect/ddfd7652-43ba-4894-a462-bee276607294?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Almost everything else in the crawl (the technicians, the drivers, the caterers, the accountants) is there by custom rather than by contract.
3. The VFX boom
The department that has seen the biggest growth in recent decades is that of visual effects. Avengers: Infinity War [ https://substack.com/redirect/99bf5136-8359-41f1-b11a-2c33e18a1a4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (2018) credited 5,109 people [ https://substack.com/redirect/7862f33f-66d8-4c7f-bade-ea76c1ed64fd?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and over half of them (2,659) were in the visual effects department [ https://substack.com/redirect/f502e52b-7e75-4f58-8a60-f07f678ce17b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Modern tentpoles farm work out to 13 or 14 VFX companies at once [ https://substack.com/redirect/b624dda4-c690-4d58-8782-bd81f59b62e9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], each of which submits its list of names.  
Across all movies the numbers are far smaller, but the shape is the same. VFX went from under half a percent of all crew credits in the 1970s to around 12% today, or roughly one crew credit in eight.
The bitter irony is that even fifteen-minute credit rolls leave people out. Studios cap how many names each VFX vendor may submit (insiders told me around 40 names is a common maximum [ https://substack.com/redirect/d77bead2-d872-46f0-aab3-60692fee739e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJU

Enterprise AI spend is now up 13x year-over-year, and enterprise leaders struggle to answer key questions such as:
* How much are we spending on AI—and is that good or bad?
* How AI-fluent is our org?
* How can we prove that AI investments are paying off?

Larridin (https://us.list-manage.com/VJyarobMiO6?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b) helps you answer these AI impact questions in three ways:
* Visibility: Larridin (https://us.list-manage.com/bADEniV9Pu0?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b) brings complete visibility to your AI token spend & attribution (https://us.list-manage.com/328tQlZxZmy?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b) , AI fluency, and AI adoption.
* Opportunity: Larridin (https://us.list-manage.com/aOWVzlJvrL4?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b) maps your workflows to identify agent automation opportunities, building your enterprise context in the process.
* Proof: Larridin (https://us.list-manage.com/FLFTNIn4QbG?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b) helps you prove your AI investments are working. We track investment in your coding agents leading to output of work and provide input to what kind of tasks are accelerating with AI and by how much.

Try Larridin now (https://us.list-manage.com/ZR_G3SyVeUx?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b)


** Preview from the Premium edition
------------------------------------------------------------


** In search of objects
------------------------------------------------------------

My friend came back from an experimental music gig recently with an audio cassette. There’s something of a trend for these, apparently, just as there is for vinyl (though without the claims about sound quality). The inconvenience is part of the point - they’re hard to digitise, which restricts circulation and means the creator retains a degree of control (this reminds me of a hip denim shop in Tokyo that called itself ‘Not Found’ so that you couldn’t Google it - you had to be in the know). They’re also a way to package up a set of tracks in a way that’s otherwise awkward without a tool like Soundcloud. And a little of it is really a pose, of course. But what’s interesting to me is that they’re something that you can actually give someone.

PREMIUM SUBSCRIBERS GET THE FULL COLUMN EVERY WEEK. TO READ THE REST, UPGRADE HERE. (https://us.list-manage.com/rDmtYXFMlTl?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b)


** My work
------------------------------------------------------------


** Ways to think about token pricing
------------------------------------------------------------

AI is in a supply crunch today, but what happens when we come out of it? How and where will supply, demand, price, capacity and capex get back into equilibrium? Today, model labs can name their price, but why won’t they end up as low-margin commodity infrastructure? LINK (https://us.list-manage.com/O0fPX70ugJT?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b)


** Another Podcast: AI Deployment
------------------------------------------------------------

Every big company deployed Copilot. Hmm. That doesn't seem to have changed everything, so now what? How does this work, how do change management and 'AI deploycos' turn out, and how does this fit into 'normal technology'? LINK (https://us.list-manage.com/Q4pV7gSLlkX?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b)


** News
------------------------------------------------------------


** Three trillion?
------------------------------------------------------------

‘Anthropic investors’ told the FT that it’s on track for run-rate revenue of $100-120bn by the end of 2026, which would be roughly the same growth rate it was at when it reported a $47bn run-rate in May (and implying maybe $70bn now?). On that basis, they propose an IPO valuation of $2tr (or perhaps $3tr, asserting a 30x revenue multiple). It would be kind of nice to see actual GAAP revenue (most reporting says the Anthropic revenue number is the gross paid by end-users to cloud providers, not the net revenue attributable to Anthropic), and getting a real sense of gross margins and the operating cost structure would be nice too.

The underlying valuation problem, as I’ve written a few times, is that we don’t know where supply and demand will get into balance (will there be a ‘dark chip’ glut?), nor how much pricing power and competitive leverage the model labs will have, nor how long we’ll keep pouring money into chasing the frontier, nor where we are in the cycle - indeed, in fairness, whether this is a cycle. If you bought Amazon in August 1999, you’d have been completely right about the future, but two years later you’d be down by 90% and you’d not be back in profit until the summer of 2007. Right now, no-one knows, and there are no certainties to anchor your analysis, which is why SpaceX share price is so volatile. LINK (https://us.list-manage.com/18dFfd_Z_MN?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b)


** Meta returns to open
------------------------------------------------------------

Meta’s AI reset continues - its new models are pretty close to the frontier, and perhaps more importantly on the ‘Paretto Curve’ of optimal price/performance. Now, just as for its Llama models last year, it’s started making them open as well, meaning that you no longer have to go to China to get a good open model. In particular, it released an open model optimised for running on a single PC.

It always seemed to be pretty clear that Meta’s strategy was for models to be commodity infrastructure sold at cost: it doesn’t have a cloud business to sell them at a profit (though that’s now being added as a backstop, at least in the current pricing crunch) but clearly it’s own business will be dependant on the capabilities that come from AI, so it wants this to be a cheap commodity, with the value coming from whatever you build on top - in Meta’s case, social and ads. Now Meta is back, but much more so than last year, releasing an ‘open’ model is also a statement about risk, and politics. Anthropic has alienated much of Silicon Valley by arguing that the risks of AI (even just things like security, without getting into AGI) means access to the frontier should be narrowly restricted, which might be a good-faith position but is also unavoidably an argument for ‘regulatory capture’ and reduced competition. Meta is pushing the opposite view - that the path to safety is to give the same
tools to everyone. Of course, that’s also the attitude it took with social. ON-DEVICE (https://us.list-manage.com/L9283O5CWhl?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b) , STRATEGY (https://us.list-manage.com/zREOr1nzyfB?e=41a75eb7a5&c2id=5fbae51e103c78da448dcb114e086e9b)


** The Bank of Jensen
------------------------------------------------------------

Two weeks ago the WSJ reported that Nvidia was going to guarantee the loans to build a $250bn OpenAI data centre; this week, apparently, that guarantee will only be for half the spend. But also this week, Nvidia announced a new $500bn AI financing JV with four giant investment firms (Apollo, Blackrock, Blackstone and KKR), plus Goldman Sachs, plus the giant developer Brookfield.

There are simple and complicated ways to explain this new JV: the simple way is that Nvidia wants to turn GPUs into fungible, tradable assets that can be used as security for loans. If you borrow money to build an AI cloud and then go bust, someone else can pick up the GPUs, so the credit risk to the finance providers is lower.

e5a04a7c591774f6.subject: She Killed Her Three Children. Is She Guilty?
e5a04a7c591774f6.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/cp/211745453

A son stabbing his mother and father [ https://substack.com/redirect/e185ce59-60c3-4add-a590-cc3743608dee?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to death. A young man killing his pregnant partner [ https://substack.com/redirect/44709588-04bc-4198-a777-148f82bc82fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] in their home. A nurse administering lethal injections to multiple infants [ https://substack.com/redirect/ebc53064-9c6d-46db-9a16-b695ed0832ee?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. There are certain crimes, incomprehensible to the average person, that prompt the tangled moral question: Was this person insane or evil?
But it’s been a long time since one of them captured the internet’s attention in the way that Lindsay Clancy’s actions have in recent days. Three years ago, she strangled her three children to death. She does not deny it. In her trial, which began a few weeks ago and is being watched live by hundreds of thousands of people [ https://substack.com/redirect/3716ab30-ac81-4f2f-ba5f-4b3bc45dfa07?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], her defense team asserts that she was so incapacitated by postpartum depression that she cannot be held accountable for murder.
Online, there has been an outpouring of support for her. Women are claiming “I could have been Lindsay Clancy [ https://substack.com/redirect/bb38c17d-8503-429e-998c-0aaa9814e314?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ],” presenting her as the innocent victim of a medical system that failed. A GoFundMe, set up by Clancy’s parents [ https://substack.com/redirect/23e02867-25ac-45b7-a452-654debda47cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], has raised $800,000—and counting. And then there are those who claim that Clancy’s ex-husband framed her for the murders [ https://substack.com/redirect/1a0e2cf7-b89f-4d6f-9694-b3cad4adc4da?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]; TikTok is replete [ https://substack.com/redirect/3ccd3d06-903d-4280-af6f-5e7d5db7d213?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] with women [ https://substack.com/redirect/adb31d63-37ad-4398-b258-9a9c2c4d6b8d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] pointing to random details from the trial and saying it’s evidence he’s abusive, as well as videos of him doing ordinary things, overlaid with spooky music, that supposedly prove he is a psychopath. These have tens of thousands of likes.
At the same time, there has been an outpouring of disgust. Clancy has been called a “monster,” and influential people have said she “deserves to die. [ https://substack.com/redirect/044561f1-ba83-45eb-86b2-a2c5a50749ad?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]”
In her essay today, Kat Rosenfield argues that all these people are trying “to box up and file away an act so incomprehensibly evil that it’s virtually intolerable to look at directly, unshrouded by either the veil of compassion or the excitement of a mystery to be solved.”
But the truth here is something far, far more complicated. —The Editors
In the matter of Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, the following facts are not in dispute: that it was the evening of January 24, 2023, when she was found on the frozen ground outside her home, back broken, bleeding from wounds on her wrists and neck, which she had inflicted on herself with a knife before jumping from a second-story window. That on this same night, her children Cora, Dawson, and Callan—ages 5, 3, and 8 months, respectively—were found in the basement, strangled with exercise bands. Cora and Dawson were pronounced dead at the scene; Callan died three days later after a brief hospitalization. That Clancy confessed to the killings [ https://substack.com/redirect/ecbb2cb3-f6c4-4617-b0fa-181987536869?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and has been on trial since late last month, now confined to the wheelchair in which she will likely spend the rest of her life, paralyzed from her chest down by the fall.
The question before the jury is not whether she did it, but whether she was sane enough at the time to be held accountable. Prosecutors, who have argued that the killings were premeditated and coolly executed, are seeking life in prison without parole [ https://substack.com/redirect/3212a29f-e671-4845-b3cb-a6febd98e6e3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]; Clancy’s defense team says that she was incapacitated by postpartum psychosis, and hence not criminally responsible.
What is in dispute, at least according to the internet, is just about everything else...

Unsubscribe https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cudGhlZnAuY29tL2FjdGlvbi9kaXNhYmxlX2VtYWlsL2Rpc2FibGU_.H4_Tz9oBq4YQ0T7fplRxLdYs1Dh-_48pEoiExO-AecY?

0010759877457fa4.subject: 700 000 Français hackés, 1,5 milliard envolé, et tout ce que l'administration nous cache
0010759877457fa4.body:
View this post on the web at https://alexispoulin.substack.com/p/700-000-francais-hackes-15-milliard

Sur la plage du fort de Brégançon, on regarde se noyer les poissons. Pendant ce temps, 700 000 Français découvrent que leurs données fiscales dorment sur le darknet, et le Premier ministre visite la Gironde calcinée depuis l’intérieur d’un véhicule aux vitres teintées. Trois scènes, un seul fil : dans ce pays, plus personne ne répond de rien.
Des adieux qui sentent le sapin
Emmanuel Macron a presque fait ses adieux à Bormes-les-Mimosas, et j’ai envie de dire : enfin un discours sincère. « Vouas allez me manquer », a-t-il lâché, mauvais acteur jusqu’au bout, gênant jusqu’au bout, magnifiques adieux. Pendant ce temps, Gérald Darmanin rallie Édouard Philippe dans un non-événement qu’une porte-parole LR elle-même refuse de qualifier autrement : c’est simplement un macroniste qui rejoint un autre macroniste, la même famille qui se redistribue les places avant que la maison ne brûle pour de bon. Et la campagne présidentielle se joue déjà sur les réseaux : Dominique de Villepin commente sa playlist Spotify comme un influenceur en manque de contenu, Laurent Wauquiez filme des TikTok vides jusque devant l’église de son mariage. Voilà à quoi ressemble la relève : des hommes qui n’ont plus rien à dire et qui le disent partout.
▶ 3:40 — Le ralliement Darmanin-Philippe et le vol de données fiscales [ https://substack.com/redirect/7988d996-096e-4575-8d5d-fc43ad420c6a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
▶ 6:47 — Villepin en playlist, Wauquiez en TikTok muet [ https://substack.com/redirect/f81e42d6-f6d9-4087-8f32-70adcfad88cd?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Le fisc troué, l’argent envolé
Des hackers qui se font appeler ZeroBytes narguent l’État français, revendent les données de 700 000 contribuables et annoncent au passage avoir siphonné 346 millions de lignes de l’Éducation nationale. Réaction du Parisien, journal de Bernard Arnault : après avoir dénoncé la faille béante de la DGFiP, l’éditorial finit par sermonner les Français sur leur exposition aux réseaux sociaux. Renverser la faute sur la victime, c’est la spécialité de la presse qui appartient à ceux qui n’ont jamais rien à se reprocher. Sauf que le vrai chiffre, le voici : 1,5 milliard d’euros dépensés en trois ans par la DGFiP pour son informatique, hors salaires, avec 5 300 agents dans la filière numérique, et le résultat tient dans une phrase. Non mais ta gueule, où est passé l’argent ? Eh bien, on ne saura pas — un audit de l’ANSSI viendra enterrer le dossier avant l’été prochain. Et Bruno Retailleau répond à ce fiasco par un « plan Vauban », une forteresse numérique promise avec le sérieux de qui n’a jamais lu une facture.
▶ 13:47 — Comment les enquêteurs traquent ZeroBytes [ https://substack.com/redirect/41957b47-1360-4533-8d26-ee0010639c1f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
▶ 17:18 — Le Parisien fait la leçon aux victimes du piratage [ https://substack.com/redirect/b5c745e3-8a44-4752-bd8b-712d823af205?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
▶ 24:03 — 1,5 milliard envolé sans résultat à la DGFiP [ https://substack.com/redirect/731d6cfc-9794-4cb6-9c92-e607920c567b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Lecornu, vitres teintées et vérité tue
Sébastien Lecornu se rend au Porge après les incendies, entouré de six ministres, un fonds de 12 millions d’euros et quelques exonérations de cotisations en poche — l’aumône habituelle. Mais l’homme qui avait traité les habitants sinistrés de complotistes reste prudemment derrière les vitres de son véhicule, évitant tout contact avec une foule à qui il doit pourtant des comptes. En conférence de presse, il jure n’avoir rien à cacher sur l’absence de veille aérienne révélée par Mediapart. On le dit beaucoup, pour un homme qui n’a rien à cacher.
▶ 27:17 — Lecornu évite la foule au Porge [ https://substack.com/redirect/08ab587d-7074-4667-abd3-3a5249e07859?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
▶ 33:08 — « Rien à cacher » face aux accusations de Mediapart [ https://substack.com/redirect/275d7d2d-fc3a-4b02-ac3c-cf4e7cf28165?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Sécheresse, vipère et une nouvelle maison BHL
Annie Genevard décrit sur France Info une agriculture ravagée par la canicule, dernier étage d’un quinquennat qui empile les crises climatique, énergétique et morale sans jamais en payer le prix politique. Manon Aubry, elle, s’est fait mordre par une vipère — moins de 300 cas par an en France, et il fallait que ça tombe sur une insoumise, ce qui ne manquera pas de faire rire Sophia Aram. Pendant ce temps Olivier Nora, évincé par Vincent Bolloré, lance sa maison d’édition et choisit pour coup d’envoi Bernard-Henri Lévy et Delphine Horvilleur — la rupture avec l’ancien monde version rentrée littéraire.
▶ 1:00:02 — Genevard et le bilan XXL des crises du quinquennat [ https://substack.com/redirect/f96de9d6-9019-4e1d-8dc5-b904cfd36282?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
▶ 1:13:46 — Manon Aubry mordue, Olivier Nora mise sur BHL [ https://substack.com/redirect/af429af3-7895-4ec1-8e9f-f5b822f0a5c0?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Un État qui perd 1,5 milliard sans détecter une faille, un Premier ministre qui se planque derrière une vitre, un président qui fait ses adieux en creux : la rentrée politique n’a pas commencé, elle achève simplement ce qu’elle avait déjà commencé à démolir.
Vidéo intégrale : La vidéo [ https://substack.com/redirect/7ab9761d-4c48-45f6-b538-6759fa59d0e9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Toutes les revues de presse : Toutes les revues de presse [ https://substack.com/redirect/6bf2ceb7-31b3-42be-b621-c6d8bb6c7f09?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Patreon : Patreon [ https://substack.com/redirect/869d1412-82af-4483-9391-5a3faf705e3e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Tipeee : Tipeee [ https://substack.com/redirect/eed6d29a-ecb1-4449-9d6f-9651eb37bb04?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Le site : Le site [ https://substack.com/redirect/17665e12-d397-40d7-80a2-4dc1035fe901?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
EDITO
Un État qui filme ses exploits et perd ses fichiers
Un groupe qui se fait appeler ZeroBytes affirme avoir dérobé, après les fichiers du fisc, les données personnelles de millions d’élèves au ministère de l’Éducation nationale. Et la réponse qui nous est faite, celle que la presse relaie avec le plus grand sérieux, tient dans un titre que je recopie tel quel parce qu’il dit tout : « que faire (et ne pas faire) si vous faites partie des personnes concernées »...

b28a758840e103df.subject: The Cap Table Never Lies
b28a758840e103df.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ef42ef52-a1e9-4d50-a939-4c3e6c355e42/Newsletter_Thumbnails__1200_x_630_px__copy_3.png?t=1787009899)
Caption: 

———————————————————————————

**PRODUCT HUNT — LAUNCHING SOON **🙌

The 1752vc Pitch Deck Analyzer goes live on Product Hunt soon. Get on the launch list and we'll send you the link the moment we're live — plus **5 free deck reviews** if you join the conversation on the day.

👉 _**[Count me in](https://share.hsforms.com/2qAL5cp_9RaORTQVHwr4tpwr18dy?utm_source=vc_unfiltered&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ph_waitlist)**_

———————————————————————————

# **The Cap Table Never Lies**

The deck is a sales document. It's polished, rehearsed, and designed to make you feel something.

The cap table is the confession.

It's the one artifact a founder can't spin. Who owns what. Who left. Who got greedy. Who didn't read the SAFE they signed. Every decision the team ever made about money and control is sitting right there, in percentages, waiting to be read.

So I read it first.

And more often than you'd think, the round is dead before the founder finishes slide three — because the math on the cap table already says no.

## **Know What Healthy Looks Like**

You can't spot a red flag if you don't know the baseline.

Per Carta's 2026 data, the median founding team still owns about 56% of the company at seed. By Series A it's 36%.Investors cross the 50% ownership line somewhere between A and B. By Series C, the founders collectively own _less than the employee option pool._

That's the normal curve. Founders give up roughly 20 points a round in the early innings and that's _fine_ — that's the deal.

Here's why the baseline matters: if a team is sitting at 30% founder ownership at the seed — before they've raised the round you're being pitched — they're already more diluted than a team that's _closed_ its Series A. The tank is half-empty and the car hasn't left the driveway. No amount of TAM fixes that.

## **The Five Red Flags I Walk On**

**1. Dead equity.** A departed co-founder still holding 25%, contributing nothing, unreachable on a good day. This is the killer. Dead equity is a tax on everyone who comes after — every future investor, every employee, every founder still in the trenches is funding a ghost. If there's no vesting and no cliff, that "25% to the guy who left in month four" is now a permanent line item nobody can scrub. I'm not buying into a company that's already paying rent to someone who quit.

**2. Founders already too thin.** Too many prior rounds, a brutal low-cap first SAFE, an option pool carved straight out of their slice — and suddenly the people doing the work own a sliver. Here's the reality: a founder with too little equity is a flight risk with a desk. If the math means they can't get rich even if this works, they'll leave the second it gets hard. I'm not underwriting motivation that's already been engineered out of the company.

**3. The investor who owns too much.** An angel or a prior fund holding 30–40% from a desperate early round. It feels like someone else's problem until it's yours. An over-owning early investor blocks the next round, scares off the lead, and leaves founders with no room to be motivated through the dilution ahead. Control concentrated in the wrong hands at seed is a structural defect, not a detail.

**4. The mess.** Handshake equity. "We'll clean it up before the round." Promised points with no paper. Verbal advisor deals. A cap table that doesn't reconcile. The mess itself is the signal — it tells you how this team handles the things that matter when nobody's watching. If they can't keep their own ownership straight, what else is duct-taped together?

**5. The crowd.** Forty SAFEs, no lead, no one accountable, a party round stitched together from everyone who'd write $10K. Which brings us to the real question.

## **When Is It Too Crowded?**

A crowded cap table isn't just administratively annoying. It's a signal_._

When a round is a patchwork of tiny checks and no lead, it usually means one thing: the smart money looked and passed. Nobody had the conviction to anchor it, so the founder duct-taped a round together from friends, family, and anyone with a checkbook. That's not validation. 

One caveat, because founders over-rotate on this: a point or two at the early stage is noise. If giving up an extra 1% is the difference between closing the round and not closing it, give up the point and close. A live company with a slightly uglier cap table beats a dead one with a pristine one. Optimizing dilution to the decimal while your runway burns is how founders lose the company trying to save the equity.

So it's not the small points. The harder ceiling is structural.

A founder needs to walk into Series C still owning enough to _care._ Work backwards from there through the dilution curve, and it's the _big_ mistakes that compound against that number — the dead equity, the over-stuffed option pool, the early investor who took 35%. So the question isn't "is there room for my check" — it's "is there room for my check AND a motivated founder three rounds from now?"

When those two can't both be true, the cap table is full. Not because of cap space — because of _incentive_ space. A new investor can't join a company where the founders have already been diluted out of caring, because you're not buying equity at that point. You're buying a team that's quietly checked out.

## **"But Great Companies Have Ugly Cap Tables"**

Fair pushback. Plenty of monsters were built on messy cap tables. Founders who gave away too much early and still won. Over-index on ownership percentages and you'll pass on a generational company because the spreadsheet offended you.

True. The cap table is necessary, not sufficient. A clean cap table on a vitamin is still a no, and a messy one on a painkiller can still be a yes.

But. A red flag on the cap table is rarely _just_ about the equity. Dead equity tells you the founder avoids hard conversations. A crowded round tells you better investors passed. A founder who can't explain their own dilution tells you they don't understand the instrument they signed. The percentages are the symptom. Judgment is the disease you're actually diagnosing.

## **The Bottom Line**

**Founders:** open your cap table before you open your deck. Kill the dead equity. Put real vesting on everyone. Clean the mess. Know your fully-diluted number and be able to defend every line. If you can't explain your own cap table in two minutes, no investor will explain a check to their LPs.

**Investors:** read the cap table first, not last. It's the cheapest diligence you'll ever do and the most honest document you'll ever get. The deck tells you what the founder wants to be true. The cap table tells you what _is._

A pitch is a story a founder tells you.

The cap table is the story they already lived — and it doesn't know how to lie.

e74f103e966069fa.subject: Announcing Lenny’s Jobs: The best place in the world to find, vet, and land your dream job
e74f103e966069fa.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/announcing-lennys-jobs-the-best-place

👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs [ https://substack.com/redirect/e5d70201-b992-4279-a78c-e9743c25a144?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] | Lenny’s Podcast [ https://substack.com/redirect/8d91c999-72ed-4a49-86f4-5e7f2a5607bb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] | How I AI [ https://substack.com/redirect/2c7b57f9-3f34-413e-a27e-530a754b7ffa?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] |  Lennybot [ https://substack.com/redirect/626b7303-ee0e-4d86-8d16-71b8db8cafe5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] | Become an AI-Native Builder [ https://substack.com/redirect/72fd8551-d11f-435d-89e9-450c29fbdac5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and some other favorite AI/PM courses [ https://substack.com/redirect/d8e2a053-f860-4ef2-8790-3416b0857957?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Factory, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, PostHog, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more [ https://substack.com/redirect/6516fbce-9d12-43c9-ab75-9370b11d6b9a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
My goal is to help you succeed in your career.
I’ve spent thousands of hours on my newsletter and podcast sharing advice on how to get better at your work. But all that advice doesn’t mean much if you don’t actually have a job—or work you’re excited about.
Over the past six months, I’ve been thinking long and hard about what more I can do to help people who are struggling to find a job they love.
Today I’m excited to announce the launch of Lenny’s Jobs [ https://substack.com/redirect/e5d70201-b992-4279-a78c-e9743c25a144?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—the best place in the world to find, vet, and land your dream job 🙌
What makes Lenny’s Jobs unique and awesome:
A laser focus on four builder roles at tech companies: product management, engineering, design, and growth/marketing. We focus exclusively on these roles because they’re what most of you are looking for—and because these roles are starting to meld together. We aggregate open roles from top startups and big tech companies, and unlike any other job directory, we vet every company we include and filter out ghost roles and generic staffing-agency posts. This is the highest-quality directory of open tech roles you’ll find anywhere.
Unlisted roles you won’t find on any other job site. Every month I poll my audience on X [ https://substack.com/redirect/3e74a139-52f5-4386-8edc-1e7b196ab0b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and LinkedIn [ https://substack.com/redirect/e01eb152-5545-4f84-a66b-e2776e6b9379?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] for roles they’re hiring for, many of which aren’t listed elsewhere. Along with submissions from our private reader Slack community, we integrate these roles into the directory. Look out for the “Lenny’s Community” tag in the feed.
The Lenny 100 [ https://substack.com/redirect/9db1890f-cdfe-42f9-9b23-26a7d6a3a182?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. To help you prioritize your search, I’ve curated a list of the top 100 companies I’d most want to join if I were looking for a job. These are companies that IMHO have the highest talent density, are tackling the most ambitious problems, have the biggest upside potential—and are actively hiring. I’ll update this list regularly.
Custom-built AI tools embedded within each job post. For every role, you can quickly rate your fit, prep for the interview, develop an outreach plan, customize your resume, and more. I’m really excited about the potential here.
A custom-built AI interview and career coach [ https://substack.com/redirect/d874ce24-c334-477b-b981-cc7473ee6fe5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Incorporating Noam Segal’s incredible set of AI skills [ https://substack.com/redirect/36b50673-12ab-451a-a968-3620874452a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that readers have been raving about, the AI coach will help you with everything from building your pitch to doing mock interviews to analyzing and debriefing to handling compensation conversations and negotiating job offers. I don’t believe there’s anything out there like this, and we have some big ideas for where this coach can go. Try it out [ https://substack.com/redirect/d874ce24-c334-477b-b981-cc7473ee6fe5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]!
An AI agent that emails you the best new jobs for you [ https://substack.com/redirect/48732183-7c3e-4860-a3a0-6d77eca906b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Tell us what you’re looking for and we’ll automatically notify you of newly posted jobs that would be a great fit. Set it up once and you’re all set. This is the only feature available exclusively for paid subscribers.
Rich company data and tech-specific filters. Every job post includes up-to-date data on company funding, layoff history, headcount growth, compensation, and employee sentiment, so you can quickly evaluate opportunities without tab-hopping across six different sites. Plus, more than 100 tech-specific search filters—including investors, valuation, and tech stack—help you find exactly what you’re looking for.
Curated interview and career resources [ https://substack.com/redirect/f9c8fc56-677c-4c32-b718-a03b90c39005?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. I’ve organized a small but powerful collection of my favorite third-party content, tools, and courses that have moved the needle for many people I know on interview prep, speaking confidence, choosing where to work, and more. I also share my favorite podcast episodes and newsletter posts on career and interviewing advice.
The site is free to use (and will continue to be), but paid Lenny’s Newsletter subscribers get higher AI feature limits, unlimited personalized results, and the proactive AI agent that notifies you about new jobs. To activate these benefits, first create a Lenny’s Jobs account, then link your paid subscription here [ https://substack.com/redirect/c43e126b-d8fd-4523-a6ce-a0a4a9e1f887?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
A huge shout-out to Amit Taylor [ https://substack.com/redirect/c9f3cc26-d870-4482-924e-f84de6194ebf?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], founder of TrueUp [ https://substack.com/redirect/8d4a1eca-f491-4945-a4ea-cefc3b13176b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], who I’ve partnered with on numerous State of the Product Job Market [ https://substack.com/redirect/3906da1a-dfaa-465d-a90c-88b42f1052d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] reports, for building this site with me. Also, a big thank-you to Ben Erez [ https://substack.com/redirect/fa226abb-88c6-407e-8743-4d4fe8a382a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], Tal Raviv [ https://substack.com/redirect/7674a6be-59a6-4c9c-9fac-1a0a98819eba?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], and Noam Segal [ https://substack.com/redirect/64d02833-ebc9-41e5-91bd-0bb65418c690?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] for tons of great feedback as this came together. We’re excited to get your feedback and keep making it better and more useful to you. And we’ve got some big plans:
Integrated white-glove recruiting services: direct intros between standout candidates and great comp

32542b59b38108f2.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.bensbites.com/p/do-you-use-a-personal-agent

Hey folks,
I want to know who uses agent products as a ‘personal agent’. ie organise stuff for you, things outside of work, handling email, doing stuff on your computer, etc.
- answers revealed in Thursday’s post.
Ben’s Bites is brought to you by Cloudera [ https://substack.com/redirect/3b6e9d2c-d87c-46cb-83e8-2d04d2cf8d5e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
A staggering 95% of organizations have delayed AI projects due to poor governance and compliance issues. So, what needs to change? Read up on exactly that in Cloudera's newest survey, The Great AI Re-Architecture [ https://substack.com/redirect/3b6e9d2c-d87c-46cb-83e8-2d04d2cf8d5e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Headlines
Grok Bot is taking over a lot of the ex-OpenClaw crowd. Just like the last cycle, there’s already a social feed for Grok Bots [ https://substack.com/redirect/40622e36-47da-48f3-92e8-3905000d0be1?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that you can’t read (easily) as a human. Hermes Desktop, another work-with-agent app, also launched a Bot mode [ https://substack.com/redirect/7d9f2a23-0928-4f52-9a26-6cacfb773835?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to mimic the UX of Grok mode. 
Grok bot in action:
enterprise GTM at SpaceXAI [ https://substack.com/redirect/3229e13f-83f3-46b3-b86f-3462a2309156?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
a new chief of staff [ https://substack.com/redirect/c437cefc-ee74-465d-a89c-d53a1d73386f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Marie Kondo for your inbox [ https://substack.com/redirect/13e9ff91-fd18-4fe2-80f7-4966a160a3bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
run admin for a SaaS business [ https://substack.com/redirect/e1324380-c563-4858-b1a3-e50e3c7b3903?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
helping a plumbing company owner [ https://substack.com/redirect/44b4c49c-aad8-40fb-96b7-89a2c7e6042a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Computer history in Codex/ChatGPT [ https://substack.com/redirect/576dd30a-bb35-4738-9448-b5887fc126d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] -  New feature that turns your activity across apps and websites on your desktop into memories and a timeline for reference when you ask it to do something (remember the limitless app?). It’s opt-in via settings. Explainer [ https://substack.com/redirect/11b10c77-1b01-4ad0-9d3d-ce39ecf9ad3d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] of how it works and an example you can try [ https://substack.com/redirect/c0790a16-6f62-45b3-acbd-940cb3b1a32b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
More Codex:
How to enable a 1M-token context window [ https://substack.com/redirect/9228a56e-6fcf-43a4-bd13-ddc8fe56d3aa?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] for Sol. (I wouldn’t bother - the default is there for a reason)
Ultrafast GPT-5.6-Sol [ https://substack.com/redirect/c483b11a-784f-4766-860f-f07322069fe1?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] in the API for select customers.
New in Claude Code:
/design skill [ https://substack.com/redirect/9161da94-cbd4-42b6-980d-660060eb38ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] creates editable UI artboards where you can pick a direction and tweak it visually (just like Claude Design). Once you’re happy, Claude Code can implement it.
Hit your limits? Set up auto-continue [ https://substack.com/redirect/6de727da-c421-437d-88e8-c307eb2dd9ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] for when the timer resets.
Google released Gemini 3.7 Flash [ https://substack.com/redirect/816c030b-579e-4c13-9d70-b49a2de5a166?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], three weeks after 3.6 Flash. Big improvements on benchmarks (better than GPT-5.6 Terra and Sonnet 5). Flash 3.7 and 3.6 are 50% off till the end of the year.
My feed
Now that Airtable’s been acquired, Google Sheets is dancing on its grave w/ Sheets Canvas [ https://substack.com/redirect/4a71c0c5-3dd9-4d29-aac3-5c8cad8e1189?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] - apps inside Google Sheets that sync with your data.
A little Mac tool to schedule boring tasks [ https://substack.com/redirect/f5d24d3d-8582-44ab-9780-7ec378266cff?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] & headless agents.
GitHub was down (again) yesterday, and Cursor launched Origin [ https://substack.com/redirect/b6bca019-2cac-434d-947d-021316d1976e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] - their competitor. Timing’s phenomenal - I half think they had it ready just for when GitHub went down, because it’s happening a lot atm.
Theo Browne broke down his AGENTS.md and SKILLS.md files [ https://substack.com/redirect/a987316b-5e76-4f2a-a1ea-47bd6b0cec7f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Which reminds me, I should do this too (again).

93bd1a8f4142e433.subject: The Surveillance Camera America Loves to Hate. Plus. . .
93bd1a8f4142e433.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/p/the-surveillance-camera-america-loves

It’s Tuesday, August 18. This is The Front Page, your daily window into the world of The Free Press—and our take on the world at large. Today: Aaron MacLean on the two ticking clocks that will decide the Iran war. Jacob Siegel says the U.S. and Israel are drifting apart—and that’s good. Coleman Hughes on Jason Arday and who gets anointed a black intellectual. And much more.
But first: One town’s war over America’s most-hated surveillance camera.
Move over, data centers. There’s a new third rail uniting the populist left and the don’t-tread-on-me right. It’s called the Flock camera, and it’s reading your license plate to assist with local law enforcement efforts.
Depending on your politics, the cameras are either making streets safer, or building a high-tech surveillance apparatus whose growing power is ripe for abuse. There is evidence to support both of these claims. Flock cameras have already stopped or helped solve [ https://substack.com/redirect/7df22264-8559-428d-9182-7a97f0187880?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] more than 700 crimes—including 79 homicides. But the tool is not without its dangers. Police officers have been charged with or accused of illegally using [ https://substack.com/redirect/04dcfd5d-81fc-406d-af46-d5c4d0a44aff?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] Flock cameras to stalk their ex-girlfriends. And in 2023, two New Mexico women were arrested at gunpoint [ https://substack.com/redirect/6b7303cc-c710-403f-915b-fb656bc545d4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] after a Flock camera mistook a 2 on their vehicle’s license plate for a 7.
To make sense of the war over Flock, River Page traveled to Troy, New York, a town of about 50,000 residents, where locals are fighting over a law that would restrict how Flock’s camera data can be stored and used. The mayor, who opposes the bill, sees it as a thinly veiled “pro-crime” effort to defund the police. Other residents claim they’re being spied on and have resolved to “get rid of Flock through policy or force.”
Flock, River writes, has become a totem of what these residents—and many other Americans—view as “a ruthless, anti-democratic tech industry dead set on remaking the world for its benefit by forcing AI and mass surveillance down everyone’s throats.”
In his dispatch today, River delivers the full picture. It’s a complicated story about trust and the tug of war between a politics that won’t tolerate injustice and one that won’t tolerate disorder. How much crime are we willing to endure in the name of privacy? Or, put differently, how much freedom are we willing to give up in the name of safety?
—Josh Code
In Iran, Trump Is Watching Two Ticking Clocks
For all the ink spilled over the Iran war, only two numbers truly matter, says Aaron MacLean. For one, there’s the outflow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz—which may actually be greater than we think, allowing gas prices to stabilize while Trump turns up the heat on Iran. But the second number is a countdown to January 3, 2027, when a new U.S. Congress takes office—likely a much more Democratic one—and begins to make it much harder for Trump to keep fighting. Read Aaron’s latest column on the crucial numbers squeezing Trump, and whether or not he can bring Iran to its knees before time runs out.
And don’t miss Aaron’s podcast today, School of War, with Pennsylvania senator Dave McCormick on why the right needs a better answer to socialism, lessons in modern warfare from his recent closed-door meeting with Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelensky, and why he regrets his 2002 LA Times op-ed supporting the Iraq War: “I was completely wrong.”
MORE FROM THE FREE PRESS
THE NEWS
Heroes actress Hayden Panettiere died Sunday at 36 [ https://substack.com/redirect/c8c5f2bf-5207-46de-849a-6cec9afabc4f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina apartment where she was temporarily staying. Authorities found no signs of foul play, though her cause of death is still under investigation.
The Supreme Court declined a second time [ https://substack.com/redirect/ae82da67-f061-4e31-bd6b-6bab73a1d9b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to take up Donald Trump’s bid to toss a $5 million verdict finding he sexually abused the writer E. Jean Carroll, rendering the judgment final. His lawyers are still fighting a separate $83.3 million he owes Carroll in a defamation case on the grounds of presidential immunity.
Jared Kushner spent four hours [ https://substack.com/redirect/ce6941b8-a07c-45d9-8a03-c9e7e3aed241?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] on Monday urging a skeptical Benjamin Netanyahu to test whether Hamas will actually disarm per Trump’s Board of Peace plan. As the two met, the President told Fox News he wants Israel to halt its air strikes on Gaza.
Luigi Mangione’s trial in New York state court, set for September 8, was effectively postponed [ https://substack.com/redirect/e6e6ba34-cd08-41e5-8b0e-26e9e1a422fa?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] by a New York judge yesterday to allow time for the prosecution to respond to Mangione’s motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds. On Friday, Mangione pleaded guilty to fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
The House Ethics Committee announced Monday [ https://substack.com/redirect/5b1895d3-0ed0-4e77-adda-996aaec43cc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] it is investigating Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat, over allegations of sexual misconduct. Gomez admitted to “personal mistakes outside my marriage,” but maintained that all acts were consensual.
Trump’s approval rating has fallen [ https://substack.com/redirect/c1966f4d-2298-43ce-9074-882d680054e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to 33 percent, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll—the lowest so far in his second term. Animating the disapproval is soaring gas prices caused by the Iran war, which only one in five Americans think has been worth it.
Opening statements in the trial for the murder of Tupac Shakur began Monday [ https://substack.com/redirect/be8a0fd9-46a2-4e02-ab1d-6634f7523b38?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], nearly 30 years after the rapper was gunned down on the Las Vegas Strip. Prosecutors called the drive-by an “act of revenge” by defendant Duane “Keffe D” Davis, claiming he incriminated himself in his own memoir.

7a48f88e5a27e4de.subject: Et si l'accès à l'IA était considéré comme un droit plutôt qu'un privilège ?
7a48f88e5a27e4de.body:
View this post on the web at https://iaethiqueinsider.substack.com/p/et-si-lacces-a-lia-etait-considere

Chers Insiders,
Mark Zuckerberg a publié le 10 août un texte de 6 500 mots intitulé « The Future is for Everyone » [ https://substack.com/redirect/45c8c59a-f03d-4ca6-bb1b-e51f27e68963?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] : une superintelligence personnelle pour des milliards de gens, gratuite dans sa version de base.
Personne n’achète sa sincérité. Le texte est plat, sans âme, et il arrive au moment où Meta court derrière les laboratoires qu’il décrit lui-même. En 2019, le même auteur annonçait « The Future is Private ». Cet été, un tribunal du Nouveau-Mexique condamnait Meta [ https://substack.com/redirect/56177a89-27cd-41a9-827a-146bcb6520e3?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] à 567 millions de dollars pour les préjudices subis par des mineurs sur ses plateformes.
La vision, elle, me va très bien. Une IA distribuée, qui tourne en local, qui ne fait pas remonter mes données chez un conglomérat, c’est ce qu’il faut viser. Je pense que l’IA est un bien commun, et que tout le monde devrait pouvoir y accéder à un coût raisonnable.
Ce qui veut dire la tarifer, comme on tarife l’eau et l’électricité. Et sur ce point précis, Mark Zuckerberg ne propose rien d’autre que des « enchères dynamiques » [ https://substack.com/redirect/d63db0b0-f67f-49ca-a266-2159cd25453c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] pour ceux qui voudront plus de calcul. Une enchère donne la ressource à qui la paie le plus cher.
Nous avons pourtant un modèle sous la main, et il n’a rien de révolutionnaire : la responsabilité élargie du producteur [ https://substack.com/redirect/3bcca409-6aee-4105-8460-bbfbfb1ef4b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Celui qui met un produit sur le marché finance la filière qui en traite les conséquences. Pour les emballages, ce sont les industriels qui alimentent Citeo, un éco-organisme agréé par l’État, à hauteur d’environ un milliard d’euros par an.
Le dispositif est imparfait, et les rapports officiels le disent : Citeo est piloté par ses propres contributeurs, ce qui les pousse à discuter le montant de leur contribution plus que les résultats obtenus. Raison de plus pour s’en inspirer en corrigeant ce défaut précis.
Un fonds équivalent pour le calcul, donc, qui achèterait en gros et redistribuerait à un tarif de base. Alimenté par les hyperscalers, qui vendent l’infrastructure, et par les entreprises qui occupent un maillon stratégique de la chaîne. Avec une part publique minoritaire, qui pèse peu dans le financement et beaucoup dans la gouvernance, précisément pour ne pas refaire l’erreur de Citeo.
L’outil circule déjà. Mark Zuckerberg dote d’un milliard de dollars un fonds [ https://substack.com/redirect/ae7697b4-d11c-4b94-a5ce-07cd257b009d?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] pour les communes qui accueillent ses centres de données, le même ordre de grandeur que Citeo. Connaissant le personnage, je ne lui prête aucune intention généreuse, et ça n’a aucune importance : un mécanisme se juge à ce qu’il produit. Il l’oriente vers ceux qui subissent ses infrastructures, rien n’interdit d’en construire un pour ceux qui n’ont pas accès à ce qu’elles produisent.
Un tarif ne réglera pas tout, cela dit. D’après l’index Ramp d’août [ https://substack.com/redirect/f391d850-fe5b-41a0-a8e7-862c6fbba0c5?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], l’entreprise médiane consacre 11,95 dollars d’IA par salarié et par mois, quand le premier centile en dépense 7 400. Et l’analyse relève qu’un plafond est désormais atteint sur ce que les entreprises acceptent de payer, alors même que les prix se sont effondrés tout l’été.
Baisser le prix du token ne déplace donc pas la médiane. Ce qui bloque en dessous se joue ailleurs.
Il faut aussi que le matériel et l’infrastructure soient réellement disponibles, et que les gens soient assez formés pour en tirer quelque chose. C’est la seconde mission qu’un fonds pareil aurait à financer.
Alors oui, l’accès à l’IA peut être considéré comme un droit. Un tarif de base opposable, une machine à portée de budget, la formation qui va avec. Rien là-dedans n’est hors de portée, et c’est exactement le genre de chose que l’Europe sait écrire.
Pour l’instant, on nous propose l’enchère et des échantillons gratuits. Rien entre les deux.
Maintenant j’aimerais votre avis, parce que le sujet mérite mieux qu’une seule tête. Est-ce que l’accès à l’IA vous paraît relever du même registre que l’eau et l’électricité ? Et si oui, qui devrait alimenter le fonds, et qui devrait décider du tarif ? A vos idées !

📖 Le livre : la souveraineté, ce sont deux questions
Je vous parle ici chaque semaine d’un concept du livre que j’écris avec Pierre-Louis Guhur, chercheur en intelligence artificielle, sur les world models.
Le chapitre 9 s’ouvre sur une scène que j’ai vue se rejouer plus d’une fois en mission de transformation. Un comité de direction, un contrat de cloud sur la table, et quelqu’un qui annonce que le sujet est réglé, puisque les données sont hébergées en Europe.
Il ne l’est pas. Parce qu’il y a deux questions, et qu’on les confond presque toujours.
Mon fournisseur s’entraîne-t-il sur ce que mes équipes lui envoient ? Et : une autorité étrangère peut-elle saisir ces données sans que je le sache ?
La première se règle par une clause de contrat. La seconde ne dépend ni de l’endroit où sont les serveurs, ni de la langue du contrat.
Le chapitre déroule les deux, puis descend un cran plus bas, jusqu’au logiciel qui voit passer vos données en clair pendant qu’il calcule.
